nameStory: The purple-brown urchin gets its straightforward name from its distinctive coloration - a rich purple-brown hue that sets it apart from other sea urchins along our coast. Unlike many marine creatures with confusing common names, this one tells you exactly what to look for: that unmistakable deep purplish-brown color that looks almost like dark chocolate with a hint of plum.
description: The purple-brown urchin is a spiny, globe-shaped marine animal that lives in shallow Atlantic waters along New England's coast. Imagine a tennis ball covered in sharp spines - that's the basic body plan of this sea urchin. These creatures are echinoderms, related to sea stars and sand dollars, and they spend their lives slowly crawling across rocky surfaces grazing on algae. They typically measure 2-4 inches across their round, dome-like body.

idTips.label: Purple-brown coloration
idTips.description: The unmistakable deep purple-brown color, like dark chocolate mixed with burgundy wine, covers both the body and spines

idTips.label: Dense spine coverage
idTips.description: Sharp, needle-like spines cover the entire round body - handle carefully as they can pierce skin and break off

idTips.label: Round, globe shape
idTips.description: Tennis ball-sized spherical body that feels solid and heavy when picked up (use gloves!)

idTips.label: Hard shell texture
idTips.description: Underneath the spines, the shell feels like smooth, hard ceramic with a slightly chalky texture

idTips.label: Five-part pattern
idTips.description: Look closely to see five distinct sections radiating from the top center, like slices of an orange

habitat: Purple-brown urchins live in shallow coastal waters throughout New England, typically in rocky intertidal zones and tide pools. You'll find them wedged into crevices, under ledges, or slowly moving across rock surfaces covered in seaweed and algae. They prefer areas with good water circulation and are most common in depths from the low tide line down to about 30 feet.

seasonality.spring: Most active as waters warm up, often found grazing on fresh algae growth in tide pools during low tides.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when they're easiest to spot moving across rocks and feeding during daylight hours at low tide.
seasonality.fall: Still active but beginning to seek deeper water and more sheltered spots as storms increase.
seasonality.winter: Less visible as they retreat to deeper water and more protected crevices, though still present year-round.

funFact: Purple-brown urchins are living lawnmowers of the sea - they have five razor-sharp teeth arranged in a complex structure called 'Aristotle's lantern' that can actually chew through solid rock over time, creating perfectly round burrows where they live!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with green sea urchins, but the purple-brown's distinctive chocolate-burgundy color is unmistakable once you know what to look for. Memory trick: 'Purple-brown like a plum' versus 'green like sea lettuce.'
contextualKnowledge: Despite their fearsome appearance, purple-brown urchins are herbivores that play a crucial role in maintaining healthy kelp forest ecosystems. Their spines are defensive, not offensive - they're actually quite gentle grazers that help prevent algae from overgrowing rocky surfaces.
compareHints: As the only Arbacia species in New England waters, compare it to the more common green sea urchin which is typically larger, bright green, and has longer, more flexible spines. Purple-brown urchins are generally smaller and more compact, with shorter, stiffer spines and that unmistakable dark coloration that no other local urchin species shares.
